earlier_scan.note: Extinct isolate of Louisiana; documentation limited to a c.1802 Sibley wordlist; no phonology/stress description exists.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Adai language' (accessed 2026-09-17).
sources.note: States Adai is known only from a list of 275 words recorded by John Sibley in 1804 (ms. at the American Philosophical Society); no phonology section; references Sibley 1804 ms., Grant 1995 (Siouan-Caddoan Conference paper), Campbell 1997, Mithun 1999.

In Carmen Dagostino, Marianne Mithun & Keren Rice (eds.), The Languages and Linguistics of Indigenous North America: A Comprehensive Guide, Vol. 2 (The World of Linguistics 13.2), ch. 61, 1627-1648. Berlin/Boston: De Gruyter Mouton. doi:10.1515/9783110712742-061
Martin, Jack B. 2001. Southeastern Languages. Draft ms. (dated 7-24-01) of the chapter 'Languages' for Handbook of North American Indians vol. 14: Southeast (2004). College of William and Mary.
sources.note: No phonology content for Adai: notes the 1802 Sibley wordlist, the possible Caddoan affiliation (Gatschet in Powell 1891:46; Taylor 1963a), and Sibley's report that the Adai also spoke Caddo.

sources.citation: Swanton, John R. 1946. The Indians of the Southeastern United States. Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 137. Washington: Government Printing Office. ['Adai', pp. 83-84.]
sources.note: Ethnohistorical entry; the only linguistic sentence is 'The vocabulary of their language, fortunately preserved by Sibley, shows that it differed widely from the rest of the Caddo dialects.' Classification table lists an 'Adai division' of the Caddoan stock. No phonology, no accent.

sources.citation: Lesser, Alexander & Gene Weltfish. 1932. Composition of the Caddoan linguistic stock. Smithsonian Miscellaneous Collections 87(6):1-15. Washington: Smithsonian Institution.
sources.note: Nothing on Adai phonology or prosody. The only Adai sentences: 'Adai is preserved to us in the form of brief vocabularies. Those words which can be summarily identified with Caddoan stems indicate that Adai is probably a divergent dialect of the Caddo.' Footnote: '..We have not seen this last Adai vocabulary' (the APS ms.).

sources.citation: Powell, John Wesley. 1891. Indian linguistic families of America north of Mexico. Seventh Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, 1885-86, pp. 1-142. Washington: Government Printing Office. ['Adaizan family', pp. 45-46.]
sources.note: No phonology content: synonymy with references (Gallatin 1836/1848, Latham 1846-1862, Prichard 1847, Buschmann 1859, Keane 1878, Gatschet 1884), Sibley's c.250-word vocabulary, Gatschet's comparison finding Caddoan affinities, tribal history and population.

sources.citation: Gatschet, Albert S. 1884. A migration legend of the Creek Indians, with a linguistic, historic and ethnographic introduction. Vol. 1 (Brinton's Library of Aboriginal American Literature 4). Philadelphia: D. G. Brinton. ['Adai', pp. 41-42.]
sources.note: Only a typological remark: the word list 'proves it to be a vocalic language independent of any other, though a few affinities are traceable with the Pani dialects. The orthography of that vocabulary cannot, however, be fully relied on.' Nothing on accent, stress or tone.

sources.citation: Gallatin, Albert. 1836. A synopsis of the Indian tribes within the United States east of the Rocky Mountains, and in the British and Russian possessions in North America. Archaeologia Americana: Transactions and Collections of the American Antiquarian Society 2:1-422. Cambridge.
sources.note: Nothing. Adaize mentioned only ethnographically (c. p. 116-118): 'The Adaize.. speak a language totally distinct from any other known to us'; notes Sibley transmitted the Adaize vocabulary to Duponceau. The comparative-vocabulary appendix is not in this scanned text; no remarks on pronunciation or accent.

sources.citation: Adelung, Johann Christoph & Johann Severin Vater. 1816. Mithridates oder allgemeine Sprachenkunde, Theil 3, Abtheilung 3. Berlin: Voss.
sources.note: Nothing. pp. 277-278 report (after Sibley) only that the Adayze language 'soll so schwer zu verstehen und zu erlernen seyn, dass keine benachbarte Voelkerschaft davon auch nur zehn Woerter aussprechen koenne'; no word list analysis, no accent statement.

sources.citation: Sibley, John. 1806 [this printing 1808]. Historical sketches of the several Indian tribes in Louisiana, south of the Arkansas river, and between the Mississippi and river Grand. In: American State Papers, containing authentic documents relative to the history, politicks, statisticks, &c. of the United States of America. Boston: Munroe, Francis & Parker. [Also in Message from the President communicating discoveries by Lewis and Clark, Sibley and Dunbar, Washington 1806, and American State Papers, Indian Affairs 1:721-725, 1832.]
sources.note: The primary (and only first-hand) characterization of Adai speech is impressionistic: the language 'differs from all other, and is so difficult to speak or understand, that no nation can speak ten words of it; but they all speak Caddo, and most of them French'. Nothing on accent, stress, tone or syllables.

sources.citation: Adai Caddo Indian Nation. 'Language' (Adaizan language program): reconstructed pronunciation and derived standard alphabet based on Sibley's 1804 documentation; videos at YouTube @AdaizanLanguage; Omniglot page 'Adaizan language and alphabet' (information supplied by adaizanlanguage[at]gmail.com).
sources.note: Pages read (adaicaddo.com/programs, omniglot.com/writing/adaizan.htm) give an alphabet chart and recordings but no written statement about stress, accent or tone; any such rule would be reconstructed, not descriptive.

sources.citation: Wiktionary. Appendix:Adai word list (transcription of Sibley's 1804 vocabulary as printed in Grant 1995, 'John Sibley's Adai vocabulary: a contribution to Caddoan lexicography?').
sources.note: Wordlist-only data: forms in Sibley's English-based spelling (e.g. nang 'fire', holcat 'water', naleen 'sun', hicatuck 'I'); no accent marks and no note on pronunciation, stress or tone.

sources.citation: Grant, Anthony P. 1995. John Sibley's Adai vocabulary: a contribution to Caddoan lexicography? Paper presented at the Siouan and Caddoan Languages Conference, Albuquerque. 15 pp.

sources.note: The only modern philological treatment of the entire Adai corpus; if anyone has commented on whether Sibley's spellings encode accent (e.g. doubled consonants, final -e), it would be here. Low expectation of a stress statement.
